transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-18 16:00 UTC; Duration ~55m; Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Elena Ortiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Lakeview CTO), Ravi Kapoor (Lakeview ML Eng), Jules Laurent (Lakeview Infra)

Summary: technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy, hit rates, cache key design, multi-tenant safety, and on-prem/VPC considerations. Focused on realistic hit-rate expectations, cache warming, eviction, and how quantization or model variants affect cache compatibility.

Topics: prefix caching architecture, KV cache vs prefix cache, cache-key construction, tenant isolation, eviction policies, benchmark methodology, VPC/on-prem constraints, telemetry and SLOs.

00:00 - 00:45 Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intros, this is Samir from Redwood, with Elena our SE, and then over to lakeview team?
00:46 - 01:15 Maya: hi yeah Maya here, CTO, ravi and jules are on. thanks for sync. we want to understand how prefix caching would help our multi-tenant chat pipelines and what risks are for sensitive prefixes.
01:16 - 02:05 Elena: cool, high-level first: prefix caching stores repeated prefix tokens (think system prompts, user profile info) so they don't re-run past kv compute every request. we typically see biggest wins for chat-style traffic with long static system prompts or reused instruction templates.
02:06 - 03:00 Ravi: what hit rates do you normally see? our mix: 60% assistant completions, many users share same persona templates, but also per-tenant custom prompts.
03:01 - 04:10 Elena: hit rates vary: in our hosted customers who share canonical system templates we see 30-70% hit rates on prefix cache; for highly personalized per-user prompts it's lower, 5-20%. important to measure prompt reuse cardinality. the bench script we use will estimate reuse and cold-start cost.
04:11 - 05:00 Samir: also note distinction: KV cache (model's key-value attention cache for autoregressive decoding) vs prefix/prompt caching at request level. prefix cache can precompute the model's KV state for a prefix and reuse it for later requests; but compatibility depends on model version, quantization, and even seq-length config.
05:01 - 06:00 Jules: slight clarification—if we run private/on-prem with quantized kernels, will the prefix cache be portable between nodes? we run mixed GPU fleet (some 8-bit quantized variants).
06:01 - 08:00 Elena: good question. portability depends on the representation. Redwood's prefix cache stores model-internal KV tensors in a normalized format tied to a specific runtime/quantization profile. we have two modes: portable cache keys (logical prefix hash + model version + quantization tag) which allow routing to compatible nodes, and raw cache blobs bound to a binary runtime. with mixed-quant fleets we recommend using the portable mode and only route to nodes that declare compatibility; otherwise cache misses will occur.
08:01 - 09:10 Ravi: how do you construct cache keys? we are worried about collisions and tenant leakage across multi-tenant hosts.
09:11 - 11:00 Elena: primary key is a stable hash of the prefix text (normalized: remove whitespace variance, canonicalize tokens), plus model identifier, model version, quantization profile, and tenant scope if desired. for multi-tenant safety we strongly recommend including tenant_id in the key or encrypting blobs per-tenant. we also support per-tenant namespaces so a same textual prefix for tenant A won't hit tenant B's cache.
11:01 - 12:10 Maya: that seems obvious but can add overhead. is there a trade-off between global shared cache to improve hit rates vs strict tenant isolation?
12:11 - 14:00 Elena: yes it's the main trade. Shared caches increase hit rates but require stronger access controls and can risk data leakage if prefixes contain PII. Typical enterprise approach: namespace cache by tenant by default, and optionally allow safe shared caches for non-sensitive system prompts. We also provide policy tags: mark prefix as sharable or private; the runbook will include default policies.
14:01 - 15:00 Samir: add that for streamed responses, we can pre-warm KV for top-k tokens but have to be careful with streaming latency: precomputing large prefixes helps throughput but adds a little cold-path latency for the first warm.
15:01 - 17:00 Ravi: eviction policies—LRU? time-based? we have constrained memory on our infra nodes.
17:01 - 19:00 Elena: common policies: LRU with size-based eviction, TTL for ephemeral prefixes, and prioritized resident cache for enterprise pinned prefixes. For constrained RAM we recommend a two-tier strategy: in-memory hot cache for high-QPS prefixes + on-disk cache for warm items. Redwood supports async loading to avoid blocking tails.
19:01 - 21:00 Jules: on-prem: can we encrypt cache blobs at rest and have KMS integration? we need to meet our compliance.
21:01 - 22:10 Elena: yes KMS/HSM integrations are supported in Private deployments. encryption at rest for blobs + tenant-scoped keys is possible. we log cache accesses to audit logs with masked keys. we'll share the security doc (Samir).
22:11 - 24:00 Maya: curious about benchmark methodology—what workloads do you run to measure latency/throughput improvement from prefix caching?
24:01 - 27:00 Elena: we run synthetic and replay benchmarks: synthetic to stress QPS and memory; replay uses representative prompt sets supplied by the customer. metrics: tokens/sec, p50/p95 p99 latency, average GPU mem usage, and delta in cost per 1M tokens. We also measure warm vs cold ratio and cache-hit distribution. our script will output hit histograms.
27:01 - 29:00 Ravi: sample numbers? ballpark reduction in inference time and GPU cycles?
29:01 - 32:00 Elena: ballpark: for chat with long static system prompts (500-1000 tokens), prefix caching can reduce per-request compute by 40-70% and improve throughput 2-4x depending on batching. For short prompts savings are smaller. If your reuse is high across tenants E.g., internal macros reused across many sessions, expect higher.
32:01 - 33:00 Samir: caveat: quantization/PRQ can affect numerical compatibility; we saw small variance when swapping between 8-bit kernels—still generally safe but we tag cache with quantization profile.
33:01 - 35:00 Maya: what about model rollouts and cache invalidation—how do we avoid stale prefixes when model weights change or we push new tokenizer?
35:01 - 37:00 Elena: cache keys include model version + tokenizer id. when you roll to a new model variant we automatically invalidate incompatible keys. We also expose cache-invalidation APIs and a TTL strategy. For canary rollouts we recommend warming caches on the canary nodes with a staged replay of the prompt corpus to reduce cold starts.
37:01 - 39:00 Ravi: concurrency and batching interactions—if we batch many requests with different prefixes, does prefix caching still help?
39:01 - 41:00 Elena: yes. Redwood's runtime performs continuous batching and will merge KV states for requests that share prefix states. If prefixes diverge it may reduce batch efficiency. The runtime has strategies to group by compatible prefixes to maximize throughput; we can show plots in the runbook.
41:01 - 43:00 Jules: multi-tenant safety again—what about side-channel leakage via cache timing or eviction patterns?
43:01 - 45:00 Elena: side-channels are a concern. Our recommendations: tenant-scoped cache partitions, constant-time access heuristics for sensitive prefixes, and monitoring for unusual access patterns. On dedicated/private installs you can set per-tenant quotas to avoid noisy neighbors.
45:01 - 47:00 Samir: also for enterprise customers we offer an opt-in hardened mode that disables shared caches entirely and forces per-tenant isolation; it increases memory footprint but removes a large surface.
47:01 - 49:30 Maya: ok good. About telemetry—what dashboards will you provide? we need p50/p95, hit-rate by tenant, eviction rate, cold starts, storage utilization.
49:31 - 51:00 Elena: Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route model dashboards, cache hit-rate by tenant and prefix, eviction metrics, and alerts when hit-rate drops below thresholds. We'll demo that in the pilot.
51:01 - 52:30 Ravi: any gotchas with function calling or tool/call outputs? our prompts often include function schemas.
52:31 - 53:30 Elena: function/tool calling prefixes are treated like any prefix; however we advise isolating tool schemas in their own namespaces to avoid accidental reuse across incompatible schemas. Also recommend schema version in the cache key.
53:31 - 54:30 Samir: recap and next steps. we'll send the benchmark script + security docs, Elena will prepare the runbook, Lakeview to provide prompts and tenant requirements, and we'll schedule pilot before month end. thanks.

Notes/References: benchmark repo (internal): https://drive.google.com/drive/fake-prefix-bench (shared with Lakeview after call); security whitepaper: https://redwood.example.com/security/prefix-caching; runbook placeholder: /runbooks/prefix-cache-runbook.pdf
